lead: A build and test pipeline turns one commit into a tested, versioned artifact through a fixed series of stages. It exists because people forget steps, and because rebuilding separately for each environment creates differences that tests never see. The pipeline does the same work every time, in the same order, and stops at the first failure. Teams use it on every commit, from a small npm library to a large Maven or Gradle system, and read its duration and failure rate to decide where to improve.
prereq: You need: 5.6 continuous integration and continuous delivery and 5.5 version control systems.

blocks.text: Build is the automated act of turning source files into a runnable or deployable artifact. A pipeline is the fixed order of stages that does this on a build server; the server is also called an agent or runner. A build tool knows how to compile and package one kind of project: Maven and Gradle for Java, Ant for older Java trees, npm for JavaScript, MSBuild for .NET.
The pipeline repeats the same steps for every commit, so a missing step is visible in the log, not remembered by a person.

items: Fetch the source at one commit hash.
Resolve dependencies from a local cache first, then from an artifact repository.
Compile changed modules, then run unit tests and static analysis.
Package the result and publish it once to the artifact repository with a version and build number.

blocks.text: An artifact repository is a versioned file store for build outputs and dependencies.

A pipeline should fail at the cheapest point. Put the shortest tests first: compile the touched modules, run their unit tests, then static analysis. A failure at 90 s costs less than the same failure after a 30-minute full suite.
Run independent jobs as parallel shards. Split a test suite by package or class so four runners take four quarters; the slowest shard sets the stage time.
Keep a small smoke suite on every commit. Run the full suite nightly, because it is too slow to block every change. A smoke suite is a short set of tests for the main paths, not a random sample.

A flaky test passes and fails without a code change. Move it to a quarantine lane: it still runs, but its failure does not block the main line, and it has a deadline for a fix. Never delete it as the first response, because it may hide a real defect.

Agents are the machines that run jobs. A self-hosted runner is one you own; it can keep large caches and reach a private network. A cloud runner is rented and starts clean; it is simpler but may be slower to warm. Choose by cost, data rules and special hardware.

An artifact name such as 2.3.0-231 has two parts: 2.3.0 is the release version, 231 is the build number. Publish it once and make it immutable; nobody overwrites 2.3.0-231. Staging and production deploy that same file, so a test on staging proves something about production.
Build once and promote the same artifact from dev to staging to production, changing only configuration. Rebuilding at each stop can pick a newer dependency and differ from what was tested.

Passwords, API keys and signing keys stay out of the repository. The pipeline reads them from a secret store or from environment variables injected at run time. A secret in a commit stays in history; rotate it, then remove it.

A cache holds dependencies and compiled outputs between runs. Key it on the lock file so stale dependencies are not reused. A cache must be disposable: a bad cache should slow the build, not break it.
Store the commit hash in the artifact metadata. From a production artifact you can find the exact source and the pipeline run that produced it.

Track four metrics: pipeline duration from commit to artifact; failure rate as failed runs divided by total runs; mean time to repair from red build to green; and lead time for changes from commit to production. Use them to find a slow stage or a flaky suite, not to rank people.

examples.question: A repository has 40 modules. A full CI build takes 30 min. A commit touches 3 modules. The incremental build recompiles each touched module in 45 s, then links and packages in 60 s. Find the incremental build time and how many times shorter it is than the full build. Explain the tag 2.3.0-231.
steps: Ratio: 1800 ÷ 195 = 9.2307... ≈ 9.23; the incremental build is about one-ninth of the full build.
Tag 2.3.0-231: 2.3.0 is the release version and 231 is the build number; publish once, then promote the same artifact.
examples.answer: The incremental build takes 195 s (3.25 min), about 9.23 times shorter than the full build, roughly one-ninth; the tag 2.3.0-231 is release 2.3.0 with build number 231.
examples.check:
modules_touched = 3
sec_per_module = 45
link_package = 60
full_minutes = 30
incremental_seconds = modules_touched * sec_per_module + link_package
incremental_minutes = incremental_seconds / 60
ratio = full_minutes * 60 / incremental_seconds
print(incremental_seconds)
print(incremental_minutes)
print(round(ratio, 2))

traps: Rebuilding separately for dev, staging and production; the bytes differ, so staging tests do not prove production.
Letting tests depend on execution order or on data left by an earlier run; they pass alone and fail in the suite.
Deleting a flaky test instead of quarantining it; coverage disappears and a real defect can hide.
Putting a secret in the repository or printing it in logs; removing it later does not remove it from history.
Reading 231 in 2.3.0-231 as a patch version; it is a build number, not part of the release version.

quiz.a: An ordered, automated set of stages that turns one commit into a tested artifact.
Maven, Gradle, Ant, npm, MSBuild (any four).

quiz.q: Why build once and promote the same artifact?
quiz.a: To keep dev, staging and production byte-identical; rebuilding can change dependencies.

quiz.q: A full build takes 20 min. A commit touches 4 modules at 30 s each; link and package takes 40 s. Find incremental time and the ratio.
A test passes alone but fails in the suite. Give two likely causes and one fix.
quiz.a: Order dependence or shared data; isolate fixtures and reset state before each test.

quiz.q: Why quarantine a flaky test rather than delete it?
quiz.a: It may still catch a real defect; quarantine keeps it running without blocking, with a fix deadline.
Duration, failure rate, mean time to repair, lead time for changes.

quiz.q: What do the parts of 4.1.2-87 mean?

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry pipelines increasingly use hermetic builds, where the build has no network access and every input is declared, because it makes results reproducible. Remote build caches and build farms cut repeated compilation across many developers. Supply-chain security adds signed provenance so a deployed artifact can be traced to its source and build. Search for hermetic builds, remote cache, SLSA provenance and DORA metrics.
